name: Low folate in mothers at conception may cause brain damage to babies

content.text: Organised by the Pakistan Nutrition and Dietetic Society in collaboration with AKU, the seminars were held under the Continuing Nutrition Education Seminar Series 2006 in the month of March, focusing on providing current scientific information regarding nutrition on topics particularly relevant to women's health.

Dr Qureshi described the devastating effects of folate deficiency in the mother on the foetus. This occurs in the first 27 days of pregnancy. She pointed out that unfortunately by the time the woman realises that she is pregnant, the damage may already be done to the foetus. "Therefore it is important to ensure that women of child bearing age are educated regarding the good food sources of folic acid (B vitamin) such as green leafy vegetables and fruits and encouraged to include them in their diets," she said.
Dr Qureshi elaborated upon the high mortality and morbidity associated with pregnancy in Pakistan and emphasised the role of good nutrition in ensuring the proper development of the foetus.

Sumaira Nasim, Senior Lecturer Baqai University and a senior member of the Pakistan Nutrition and Dietetic Society, pointed out that it was not enough to worry about the woman's nutrition only during pregnancy. She talked about the intergenerational effects of malnutrition on pregnancy outcomes saying that women who are malnourished as children grow up to be malnourished females and improving diet during pregnancy is not enough to undo the harm of deprivation throughout life. Thus the nutrition of the girl child must receive proper attention if we wish to decrease maternal morbidity and morality, she said.

She pointed out that low birth weight remains an ongoing problem in Pakistan with 30-40 % of the babies born being below 2.5 kg at birth. It is now being recognised in the scientific community that babies that have low birth weight are also at increased risk of chronic disease such as diabetes, hypertension and heart disease.

Dr Ghazala Rafique, Senior Instructor from the Department of Community Health Sciences, AKU presented a case study on Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) which is a temporary condition that occurs for the first time during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. Usually, there are no symptoms of Gestational Diabetes and it is diagnosed through blood tests at 24 to 28 weeks of pregnancy. Dr Rafique said that risk factors for developing this condition include a previous diagnosis of GDM, age over 35 years, obesity, a history of polycystic ovary syndrome and being a member of a population considered to be at high risk for diabetes that includes women of South Asian descent.

Discussing the dietary management of GDM, Ms Saima Rasheed, Nutritionist from Park Lane Hospital, informed the audience that diets containing 40-45% of total energy intake from carbohydrates have shown to reduce postprandial blood sugars. She said that the carbohydrate intake throughout the day should be distributed into three small-to-moderate sized meals and 2-4 snacks. She stressed upon the role of exercise which helps to lower both fasting and postprandial sugar levels and should be used as an adjunct to dietary management.

As a part of its social responsibility and commitment to the advancement of health research and education, AKU regularly holds seminars, symposiums and events to raise awareness about health and education related issues which are of national importance and interest.

content.title: Low folate in mothers at conception may cause brain damage to babies
content.author: volunteer.pa
content.description: "Mothers deficient in folate at the time of conception might give birth to babies with neural tube defect," Dr Rahat Qureshi, Associate Professor Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Aga Khan University stated this addressing the last event of the series of seminars on Women's Nutrition and Health held at AKU Stadium Road Campus.
